title: Modern India
summary: ## Rise of the West and British control

From 1450 the printing press, the Renaissance and Reformation and new trade routes changed Europe, which progressed in science, exploration and gunnery. The Portuguese, Dutch, French and finally the British competed for Indian trade; the British gained trade, then the country and drained its wealth. They used the many states that arose after the Mughal decline, setting one ruler against another; Tipu Sultan of Mysore tried to use the French–British rivalry but could not match their diplomacy and fire power. British domination had three phases: control of trade (buying cheap from peasants through Seths and gomastas), control of production to suit exports and destruction of Indian industries, and intensified imperialism for British economic interests. After the Battle of Plassey (1757) they became the real masters of Bengal, monopolised raw cotton and imposed heavy duties on Indian goods in Britain. With the industrial revolution Indian handicrafts lost home and foreign markets by 1813, when the Company's monopoly ended and India became an economic colony: an excellent consumer of British goods and a supplier of raw materials. Steamships, railways (first line Bombay to Thane, 1853) and the telegraph and postal service (Dalhousie, Calcutta to Agra, 1853) served British commerce but also brought Indians and ideas closer.

Agriculture was the main occupation but constant war prevented improvement. Foreign trade flourished under the Mughals (imports: pearls, raw silk, wool, dates from the Persian Gulf; coffee, gold, drugs, honey from Arabia; tea, porcelain, silk from China; luxury goods from Tibet, Singapore, Indonesia, Africa and Europe; exports: raw silk, silk fabrics, indigo, sugar, pepper and famous cotton textiles). Despite a favourable balance of trade, the economy suffered from constant warfare, revolts of Sikhs, Jats and Marathas, and invasions by Nadir Shah (1739) and Ahmad Shah Abdali (1761). Socially there was division on region, tribe, language and caste; caste rules governed marriage, diet, inter-dining and profession; science and mathematics were neglected; education was traditional, supported by local rulers and the rich, and girls seldom went to school. Hindu–Muslim relations were friendly with tolerance and shared festivals.

Women's condition was poor: the birth of a girl was thought unfortunate, child marriage and polygamy were common, there was no right to property or divorce, perpetual widowhood for upper castes (widows could not wear coloured clothes or attend marriages, their presence being inauspicious), purdah, and no education. Christian missionaries opened schools and started the printing press; English education opened the window to liberalism, rationalism, democracy, equality and freedom, and English became the lingua franca of the educated. Ram Mohan Roy, harbinger of the modern age, had Sati banned and founded the Brahmo Samaj (monotheism, against idol worship, polytheism and ritualism); Debendranath Tagore and Keshab Chandra Sen followed; it was the first organised vehicle of national awakening. Prarthana Samaj (Bombay, 1867, Dr Atmaram Pandurang; Ranade): inter-caste dining and marriage, widow remarriage, uplift of women and depressed classes. Ramakrishna Paramhansa and Vivekananda (Ramakrishna Mission): equality and oneness of religions, Vedanta. Theosophical Society (Madame Blavatsky, Colonel Olcott; Annie Besant founded the Central Hindu School). Narayana Guru (born Kerala 1854) worked for social and religious reform. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan started the Aligarh movement and the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (later Aligarh Muslim University), against purdah, polygamy and easy divorce, giving Muslims Urdu and a press. Swami Dayanand founded the Arya Samaj in 1875 ('go back to the Vedas', Satyartha Prakash, Shuddhi movement, DAV schools from 1886). Jyotiba Phule (Pune, born 1827): school for lower castes and the Satya Shodhak Samaj (1873). Pandita Ramabai: Sharda Sadan, a home for widows (1890). Maharshi Karve (Bharat Ratna) worked for women's education; the Sharda Act (passed 1929, in force 1930) set minimum marriage age at 18 for boys and 14 for girls. Ambedkar and Gandhi worked for the depressed classes (Gandhi: Harijans).

Lithography (invented 1798) allowed many copies; from about 1820 hundreds of pamphlets and books appeared, and the press became a powerful tool of public opinion and nationalism. Novels, essays and poems in Indian languages stirred nationalism: Bankim Chandra's Anandamath, Dinabandhu Mitra's Neeldarpan, Bhartendu Harishchandra's Bharat Durdasha, Lakshminath Bezbaruah (Assamese), Subramania Bharati (Tamil) and Altaf Hussain Hali (Urdu). Newspapers: Hindoo Patriot, Amrita Bazar Patrika (Bengal), Maharatha and Kesari (Bombay), The Hindu and Swadeshamitran (Madras), The Tribune, Akhbar-i-Am (Punjab).

The Indian National Congress was founded by A.O. Hume in 1885 (era of Moderates); the Muslim League was seen as the first fruit of 'divide and rule'. Home Rule Leagues (1915–16) were started by Tilak at Poona and Annie Besant at Madras. 1905–18 was the era of Extremists (Lal, Bal, Pal) with agitation against Curzon's partition of Bengal, Boycott and Swadeshi. 1919–34: Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919, General Dyer), Khilafat and Non-cooperation under Gandhi (his first triumph was the Champaran Satyagraha), Swaraj Party, Simon Commission, Nehru Report (1928), Purna Swaraj at Lahore (1929), Salt Satyagraha or Dandi March (6 April 1930) and Civil Disobedience. Government of India Act 1935; Quit India (August 1942) after the Cripps Mission; INA (Azad Hind Fauj) of Subhas Chandra Bose (1943); Cabinet Mission 1946; India became free on 15 August 1947 after partition. Independent India built a secular democratic republic, integrated the princely states and began economic planning.

objective: Answer in one word: (a) Who founded the Arya Samaj? (b) In which year was it founded?
Answer in one word: (a) Who founded the Brahmo Samaj? (b) Who succeeded him as leader?
(a) Raja Ram Mohan Roy. (b) Debendranath Tagore.
Answer in one word: (a) What is the method of printing from a prepared stone surface called? (b) Who wrote Neeldarpan?
Mark true or false: (a) The Arya Samaj opposed untouchability and polytheism. (b) Syed Ahmad Khan encouraged Muslims to join the national movement.
(a) True. (b) False – in later years he advised them not to join it.
Mark true or false: (a) Railways played a role in national awakening. (b) The East India Company's trade monopoly ended in 1813.
Answer in a phrase: (a) Why did reformers use novels, dramas and poetry? (b) Why did reformers use Indian languages?
(a) To reach and awaken the common people. (b) To make their message understood by the masses.
Fill in the blanks: Gandhi's first triumph in India was the ______ Satyagraha. The Quit India Movement was launched in August ______.
vsa: Why did the social reformers take up the cause of women on priority?
Modern education made them realise the deplorable condition of women – child marriage, polygamy, purdah, widowhood and illiteracy – and many practices were wrongly claimed to have religious sanction.
Explain Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's role in education.
He started the Aligarh movement and the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, which became Aligarh Muslim University, to give Muslims modern education in science and culture.
Name two social evils which the Brahmo Samaj sought to abolish.
Sati, idol worship, polytheism, child marriage and caste rigidity (any two).
What is lithography? How did it help the growth of Indian languages?
Lithography, invented in 1798, is printing from a specially prepared stone surface; many copies could be printed cheaply, so presses, newspapers and books in Indian languages grew rapidly.
What was the contribution of Jyotiba Phule?
He opened a school for the lower castes and women, founded the Satya Shodhak Samaj in 1873 and worked for social justice for the so-called untouchables.
Why did India become an economic colony of industrial England by 1813?

The Company's monopoly ended in 1813, Indian handicrafts lost markets to cheap British machine goods with free entry into India, while Indian goods paid heavy duties in Britain; India became a consumer of British goods and supplier of raw materials.
sa: Describe the condition of women in India at the end of the 18th century.

A girl's birth was thought unfortunate; girls were married in childhood and polygamy was allowed; women had no right to property or divorce; widows faced perpetual widowhood, could not wear coloured clothes or attend marriages; purdah and lack of education added to their hardship.
Write about the Arya Samaj and Swami Dayanand.

Swami Dayanand, a scholar of Sanskrit and the Vedas, founded the Arya Samaj in 1875 to propagate the true knowledge of the Vedas ('go back to the Vedas') and remove later evils. He opposed idolatry, polytheism, untouchability and ritualism and supported women's education; his Satyartha Prakash is the main work; DAV schools began in 1886 and the Shuddhi movement reconverted Hindus.
Explain the role of the press and newspapers in the national awakening.

Cheap printing led to journals and newspapers in every language and national literature such as Anandamath and Neeldarpan; the press shaped public opinion, criticised government policies, spread anti-British feeling and gave political education and pan-Indian consciousness.
Write a note on Pandita Ramabai or Narayana Guru.

Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922), a scholar, joined the Prarthana Samaj and started Sharda Sadan, a home for widows, in 1890. Narayana Guru (born 1854, Kerala) was a saint and reformer who worked with Chattambi Swamigal for social and religious progress and unity of communities.
la: Explain the condition of trade and commerce of India during the 18th century.

Agriculture was the main occupation but constant wars prevented improvement. Foreign trade flourished under the Mughals: India imported pearls, raw silk, wool and dates from the Persian Gulf, coffee, gold, drugs and honey from Arabia, tea, porcelain and silk from China and luxury goods from Tibet, Singapore, Indonesia, Africa and Europe, and exported raw silk, silk fabrics, indigo, sugar, pepper and world-famous cotton textiles. In spite of a favourable balance of trade the economy could not improve because of warfare, revolts of Sikhs, Jats and Marathas and invasions of Nadir Shah (1739) and Abdali (1761). European powers added instability and eventually destroyed it, though India was famed for handicrafts.
Explain the life and works of Swami Ramakrishna Paramhansa and Vivekananda.

Ramakrishna Paramhansa (Gadadhar Chattopadhyaya) taught the oneness of all religions and the equality of all. His disciple Swami Vivekananda gave final shape to his teachings and founded the Ramakrishna Mission to regenerate Indian society; he advocated liberty, free thinking and equality, promoted Vedanta as the most rational system of thought, and the Mission worked in education, relief and against caste.
Describe the impact of the British on the Indian economy.

The British first took hold of trade, buying cheap from peasants through Seths and gomastas; then controlled production to suit exports and destroyed Indian industries; after Plassey they monopolised cotton and imposed heavy duties on Indian goods in Britain. By 1813 India was a consumer of British goods and supplier of raw materials; railways, steamships and telegraph served British trade. Indian handicrafts faced extinction.
Write an essay on India's struggle for freedom (outline).

The Congress was founded in 1885 (Moderates); the Extremists (Lal, Bal, Pal) led Swadeshi and Boycott against the partition of Bengal (1905); Home Rule Leagues (1915–16); under Gandhi came Champaran, Non-cooperation, Khilafat, Civil Disobedience and the Dandi March (1930); Purna Swaraj was declared in 1929; the Quit India Movement was launched in 1942 and the INA fought under Subhas Bose; after the Cabinet Mission of 1946 India became free on 15 August 1947.
